quoted_clause: 9.2K input at ~2.62 MB/KV‑token costs ~24.1 GB of cache (initial) on the 70B generation model, well within the 8×H100 node's 640 GB HBM.
observed: 24.1 GB is per request. 640 GB is aggregate node HBM. A 70B FP16 model alone is ~140 GB, leaving ~500 GB before workspace and fragmentation. At 10 rps and ~8.6 s service time, concurrency is ~86 requests, requiring ~2.1 TB of KV at 24.1 GB/request; even at 1.2 s TTFT, ~12 concurrent requests require ~289 GB KV plus weights. 'Well within' is true only for one request, not for the canonical load.
correction: Show the concurrency budget explicitly: weights + workspace + N × 24.1 GB ≤ 640 GB; compute N and compare with peak concurrency. Replace 'well within' with a scoped statement such as 'fits for a single request; the node supports roughly N concurrent 9.2K-token requests before KV pressure.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case includes weight residency, workspace, and concurrency arithmetic; no unqualified 'well within' claim remains.

quoted_clause: the incremental per-request compute cost of the 768-dim (all-mpnet) vs 384-dim (MiniLM) embedding models — a cross-model difference, not a dim-only sweep — is ~11.1 GFLOP per 64-token query (2 × params × L: 14.08 − 2.94 GFLOP, the §3(a) embedding table's own rows; a same-family 384-dim variant halves index storage (encoder compute ~unchanged)) — ~56–370 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at a realistic 30–200 GFLOP/s, but only ~1.1 ms on a ~10 TFLOP/s GPU, which is the basis the ~120 ms retrieval budget already assumes (vector search and reranking on a local GPU, Ch 4). On that basis the incremental cost stays well within the ~120 ms retrieval budget; single-core encoding fits only at the high end of that throughput range (55.5 ms at 200 GFLOP/s vs 370 ms at 30 GFLOP/s) — conditional on measured single-core throughput. The decision hinges on whether the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain (an unverified prior of a few to ~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS], domain- and corpus-specific — §5.3) translates into sufficient answer-quality improvement to justify the ~4.8×FLOP cost (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP per 64-token query, Table 5-1) — a workload-specific tradeoff, not a universal rule.

The paragraph's intellectual job is to show that the 768-dim choice is compute-justified and that the quality claim remains unvalidated, but the density obscures both points.

observed: The scope limitation is important (the formula is not the full economic comparison) but is buried in a long parenthetical at the end of a dense paragraph. A reader who skims the paragraph may miss it and treat Q* as the complete break-even criterion.
correction: Promote the scope note to a standalone sentence immediately after the formula, before the 'Below Q*' explanation: 'Note: this formula captures only the one-time training and carry cost amortized against the quality uplift. It does not include the recurring per-query savings from a shorter fine-tuned context (less retrieval, less prefill), which would lower the true break-even volume. The Q* above is therefore a conservative (higher) estimate of the queries needed to justify fine-tuning.'
acceptance_test: A reader who stops after the formula and the 'Below Q*' sentence still understands that the formula is incomplete and in which direction it is incomplete.

quoted_clause: If the workload is input-heavy (9.2K average input, 300-token output, ~30× more input than output), the system is first-order memory-capacity-bound (KV residency at the Ch 17 concurrency screen) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs — a first-order tendency to verify per workload, not a consequence of input-heaviness alone. If the workload were output-heavy, the token/FLOP mix shifts toward decode, which often makes decode bandwidth or latency critical — the actual bottleneck must be measured on the target stack.
observed: The paragraph correctly hedges both claims ('first-order tendency to verify per workload,' 'the actual bottleneck must be measured'). However, the phrase 'memory-capacity-bound' is used without the full three-bound distinction that Ch 8 §1 establishes (compute-bound vs memory-bandwidth-bound vs memory-capacity-constrained). A reader encountering this in Ch 5 (before Ch 8) may conflate 'memory-capacity-bound' with 'memory-bandwidth-bound.' The Ch 8 distinction is the correct one, but Ch 5 uses the term before it is defined.
correction: Either (a) add a brief inline definition: 'first-order memory-capacity-bound (the KV cache's HBM footprint limits how many concurrent requests fit — distinct from memory-bandwidth-bound, where the rate of HBM reads limits per-token speed; Ch 8 §1 formalizes the three-way distinction)'; or (b) rephrase to avoid the term: 'first-order limited by KV-cache HBM capacity (the per-request KV footprint constrains concurrency at the Ch 17 screen) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs.' Option (b) is simpler and avoids the forward reference.
acceptance_test: A reader who has not yet read Ch 8 can distinguish the 'memory-capacity' constraint (how many requests fit) from a 'memory-bandwidth' constraint (how fast each token is produced) based on Ch 5's text alone.
verdict_fix: Remove '10×' or introduce the industry claim earlier
verdict_evidence: ch05: '10×' only at :183 (the quote) and :59 (10× corpus size, not cost) — no 10× cost antecedent

quoted_clause: ~56–370 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at a realistic 30–200 GFLOP/s
observed: The top of the stated range (200 GFLOP/s for a single core) is close to the theoretical AVX-512 FP32 FMA peak of a high-clock core, not a realistic sustained GEMM rate. The conclusion 'single-core encoding fits only at the high end of that throughput range' depends on this upper bound, and the derived 55.5 ms figure is presented as if it were attainable.
correction: Label the range (e.g. '30–60 GFLOP/s sustained per core; ~200 GFLOP/s is the AVX-512 theoretical peak') and state the requirement directly: the query encoder must sustain ≥ ~93 GFLOP/s per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s) to fit the ~120 ms retrieval budget.
acceptance_test: The per-core rate range is labelled peak vs sustained, and the ms figures are recomputed from the labelled range.
verdict_fix: Label 30-60 sustained vs ~200 peak; state ≥92.5.

quoted_clause: The ~15% MAP gain behind this recommendation is likewise not quantified for this model pair

quoted_clause: rather than treat dimension as a cost-free or universally-better knob (see the caveat in §5.3).
observed: The caveat being referenced lives in §3(a) of this chapter. '§5.3' is ambiguous under the book's own notation: read as 'section 5.3' it points to a non-existent unit (§5 is an unnumbered bullet list); read as 'chapter 5, section 3' it points to §3 generally rather than §3(a). The same '§5.3' form is used earlier in §3(a) for the same caveat.
correction: Adopt one convention explicitly (chapter.section) and cite as '§5.3(a)' in both places; state the convention once in the front matter or a note.
acceptance_test: Every '§x.y' reference resolves to an existing numbered unit under the stated convention, and the same convention is used in every chapter.
verdict_fix: Cite §5.3(a); state the §N.M convention once.
verdict_evidence: ch5:148 '(see the caveat in §5.3)'; §5 = unnumbered bullets (no 5.3); caveat in §3(a) (ch5:61)

quoted_clause: the effective cost is ~0.40 $/tok/s, or equivalently ~2.5 (tok/s) per dollar-per-hour of budget
observed: The primary unit is dimensionally incomplete: the quantity is dollars per (token/s) per hour ($20/hr ÷ 50 tok/s = $0.40 per tok/s per hour). As written, '$/tok/s' reads as a per-token cost, which would be wrong by a factor of 3,600.
correction: Write '$0.40 per (tok/s) per hour' or '$0.000111 per token at 50 tok/s'.
acceptance_test: Every per-dollar figure in the chapter states its time basis, and the reciprocal form is used consistently.
verdict_fix: Write '$0.40 per (tok/s) per hour'.
